items.originalTitle: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
items.author: Ebony Riddell Bamber
items.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
items.summary: In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage . When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan. Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here .

items.title: First-half blitz secures Australia’s fourth straight Women’s Rugby League World Cup title
items.summary: Jillaroos retain their crown with dominant 34-10 win over Kiwi Ferns Jamie Chapman scores hat-trick before the break in Brisbane In northern Australia, they call this time of the year “the build up” – a sub-tropical rise in heat and pressure where dark clouds roil and minds melt before the heavens open. At Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium, it was Australia’s Jillaroos who brought the storm, dominating their New Zealand rivals from the get-go and raining down six first-half tries to win 34-10 and thunder their way to a fourth consecutive World Cup title. If this Australian apocalypse had a horsewoman, it was star winger Jaime Chapman. The long-striding speedster scored three sensational tries in the first half alone to take her tournament tally to 13, breaking the record for an individual at a World Cup. Chapman already has 521,000 Instagram followers around the rugby-loving world. After this try-scoring spree – she now has 18 from her 10 Tests – it’ll be a million.

items.author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
items.title: Entangled Past: how descendants of enslaved and enslavers in Grenada embarked on journey of repair
items.summary: In their book, the historian Nicole Phillip and journalist Laura Trevelyan use connected experiences to show how reparations can work in practice When the Grenadian historian Nicole Phillip opened an email from the then BBC journalist Laura Trevelyan in 2022, she uncovered a connection that stretched back centuries. Their ancestors had stood on opposite sides of enslavement in Grenada: Phillip’s among Africans forcibly taken from their homes and enslaved, Trevelyan’s among the British families who profited from a system that inflicted unspeakable cruelty and inhumanity on generations of enslaved Africans.

items.originalTitle: ‘I was nervous before my solo stay in a remote Scottish Highlands cabin – but the solitude is glorious’
items.author: Emma Gibbs
items.title: ‘I was nervous before my solo stay in a remote Scottish Highlands cabin – but the solitude is glorious’
items.summary: As a lone female traveller, the prospect of staying in a hut on Rannoch Moor is daunting, but the silence of the mountains and lochs turns out to be ‘the ultimate luxury’ In the gloaming, the trees stand dark and impenetrable on either side of the path. An owl, wide-faced and pale as a spectre, glides out of the pines ahead of me. Heart pounding, I pick up speed and continue uphill, the silence thick around me. Just a few minutes earlier, I had been scuffing my feet in the sand by the loch shore, watching as the clouds draped themselves across the top of the Grampians. In the absence of other people, Loch Laidon, silvery in the half-light, had been mine to enjoy; in the woods, however, my solitude feels unnerving.

items.originalTitle: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
items.author: Annalisa Barbieri
items.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
items.summary: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care.

items.originalTitle: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
items.author: Polly Hudson
items.title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
items.summary: As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us . Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé . We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience. A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may. My friends, it should be noted, felt the same. Thank God the heroic woman forced to endure Brand’s attack knew better.

items.originalTitle: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
items.author: Jordan Blum
items.title: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
items.summary: An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques. “As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential. He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas . This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year. But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted. “EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune . The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031. These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed moment in October of inking its largest customer. But first, let’s take a quick step back. Two years ago, The Wall Street Journal ran this headline about Egan: “He Wants to Be the Lithium King. Run for President. And Live to 150.” The wording is brash but not inaccurate—yes, he says he still wants to occupy the White House and live well past 100—and he comes across as an over-the-top tech bro. Many didn’t take him seriously. Egan went to work proving the doubters wrong. Since then, EnergyX opened its new Austin, Texas headquarters, nearly quadrupled its acreage footprint in the lithium-heavy Smackover Formation in East Texas and southwestern Arkansas, completed its Texas and Chile demo projects, and received a $225 million influx from Italian energy giant Eni. Most importantly, in October, major energy trading house Trafigura signed a $2 billion, 10-year contract with EnergyX for 100,000 metric tons of lithium from its Black Giant and Project Lonestar enterprises. “To have that type of customer is not only really encouraging for us, but also really validating to the rest of the market,” Egan said. “This is actually the single-largest DLE offtake in history. That’s a cool little feather in the cap. The major thing that investors or project lenders need to see is that type of contract.” His expectation is that more buyers will quickly follow suit, bringing EnergyX close to commencing construction. The Trafigura deal also boosts EnergyX’s pending $690 million loan with the U.S. Export-Import Bank. While EnergyX’s success is far from assured, Egan has proven his company must be taken seriously. Drilling ahead Egan’s mentor and idol is his father, Michael Egan, who became the majority owner of Alamo Rent a Car, grew the company nationally, and sold it in 1996, continuing to chair the business until 2003. Now retired, Michael Egan sits on the EnergyX board. “I’m a serial entrepreneur. My dad was a serial entrepreneur. I learned from him,” Teague Egan said. “I don’t have an engineering or a chemistry degree. I’m an entrepreneur. I’m a problem solver. I feel like I have a Ph. D. in engineering from working at EnergyX for eight years.” After growing up near Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Egan moved to Los Angeles to attend the University of Southern California. While a college student, he started a record label and sport agency. He quickly found success in music after signing the Boston rapper Sammy Adams, who hit No. 1 on the iTunes hip-hop chart in 2010. Egan said his biggest regret might be declining to sign a deal with his label and Interscope Records because Egan didn’t find much continued success in music. Then again, if he had, EnergyX probably wouldn’t exist, he said. His music profits though led him invest many of his gains. He was an early investor in Tesla in 2013 when the company still had a market cap of less than $10 billion. Today, Tesla sits above $1.5 trillion. Egan said he used some of those proceeds to help start EnergyX. Ever since, Egan has become an admitted follower of all things Elon Musk and his approach to business. And they’re both Austin, Texas-based now. “He’s transformed into arguably the greatest entrepreneur and innovator in the history of humanity,” Egan said. “People can say about what they want about his political views and stuff but, in terms of his contributions to humanity, he’s like unmatched. He’s essentially my idol other than my father. He has that same sense of curiosity and problem solving.” EnergyX Leaning into lithium Driven by EVs and now also by battery energy storage, global lithium demand has jumped more than 400% this decade, to over 1.5 million metric tons per year. By 2035, that demand could approach 4 million tons. With the lithium business focused on traditional hard-rock mining or evaporation ponds, Egan sought another way. Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium, literally waiting for the sun to evaporate the water and help filter out the lithium. Egan isn’t that patient. He jumped into direct lithium extraction technology. He didn’t invent it, but he wants to perfect and commercialize it. Using advanced filtration technology, DLE operates much like oil and gas by drilling wells, pumping out the brine water, processing and refining the lithium, and returning more than 90% of the brine underground. DLE can take two days instead of two years, although the upfront costs are extensive. But the legacy lithium industry wasn’t ready to embrace DLE, and especially not the required financial investments. “Our original business model was just to license our technology to the existing pond producers. We said, ‘Hey, we have a better mousetrap. This will be much better for you,’” Egan said. “They strung us along and, finally, we realized that, and we said we’re going to have to go acquire our own resources and vertically integrate to prove this and scale it and realize the technology.” That’s when EnergyX began acquiring its own acreage in Chile and the Smackover. Chile and Argentina count among the top lithium producers globally—with Australia and China—but the U.S. only accounts a little more than 1% of global lithium supplies. Those U.S. projects are concentrated in Nevada, including Lithium Americas’ Thacker Pass project currently under construction. EnergyX also is exploring a project in Utah. “A decade ago, the total volumes of lithium demand didn’t warrant new innovation and investment,” Egan acknowledged. Everything has changed very rapidly. But the Smackover region is believed to have the greatest potential to boom in the U.S. The challenge is the lithium is found in high concentrations within an underground aquifer that requires DLE. Vancouver-based Standard Lithium is scheduled to start construction on the first major DLE project in the Smackover early next year, at least a few months ahead of EnergyX. Because of the similarities to oil and gas, ExxonMobil and Chevron are fast followers, having acquired massive acreage footprints in recent years. “The U.S. is definitely at a tipping point for lithium production,” said Standard Lithium CEO David Park. “The area that has the greatest potential is the Smackover basin. When you think of the Smackover, you should really think of it as lithium’s Permian Basin. Through the introduction of relatively novel technologies, we’re able to open a once non-economic resource in a manner that can bring on projects of scale with world-class economics.” While there’s room for multiple winners, Egan said he’s convinced EnergyX’s in-house lithium filtration technology will make it the choice producer for customers going forward. The lithium reserves in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia in South America have fewer impurities than in the U.S., Egan said, but the Smackover is still a fantastic resource, and the U.S. needs to build up its own domestic supplies. Long-term lens Even though EV sales are slower in the U.S. than the much of the rest of the world, Egan sees the path forward from his Austin hub in a city that serves as the unofficial lab for self-driving vehicles and robotaxis—nearly all of which use lithium-ion batteries. Early this month, Tesla said it is discontinuing the costly Cybertruck to make way for the self-driving Cybercab, while Waymo, Avride, and Zoox are all betting on robotaxis. Egan sees them daily. “Living in Austin is seeing the future, and that is only going to spread.” That future requires EnergyX growing exponentially, he said. “I’m a long-term goals kind of guy. A lot of people call me the ‘king of lithium.’ We’ve taken steps, especially this year, to continue to build upon that. Our goal is to be producing between 500,000 and a 1 million tons of lithium per year by 2040 and become the biggest lithium company in the world.” And, yes, after that, he does still have his eyes set on the White House and running for president. “That’s still a long-term goal. I don’t think it’s unreasonable. The mindset of America has changed a lot over the past 10 years into who can lead the country. With [President] Trump, for better or worse, anything is possible now.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
